When you use "jockey" as a verb, it always involves skillful, strategic maneuvering — moving yourself, something, or someone cleverly to gain an advantage or to handle a difficult situation. There is almost always a sense of effort, competition, or cleverness baked into the word. It is never passive or accidental; jockeying is always deliberate.

1. To maneuver something carefully in a physical, tight, or tricky situation

Here, "jockey" means to handle or move something with careful skill — often in a small or restricted space, requiring precise, back-and-forth adjustments.

Examples:

  • She jockeyed the sofa through the narrow hallway. (She carefully moved it, adjusting angles repeatedly to make it fit.)
  • He jockeyed his truck into the tight parking spot. (He made small, controlled moves — forward, backward, turning — to squeeze it in.)
  • The pilot jockeyed the plane into position on the runway.

What makes it "jockey" and not just "move"? The word implies that the task required skill and careful adjustment, not just a single simple movement. There's a sense of working against some constraint — a tight space, an obstacle, a difficult angle.

2. To compete cleverly and strategically for a better position or advantage

This is the far more common and important meaning. Here, "jockey" describes the act of making smart, tactical moves to get ahead of others — to gain power, a better spot, more influence, or any kind of edge. It almost always happens in a competitive environment where others are trying to do the same thing.

Examples:

  • The politicians were jockeying for the top position in the party.
  • During the meeting, everyone was jockeying to sit near the director.
  • The two companies are jockeying for control of the market.
  • Runners jockeyed for position at the start of the race.

The most famous phrase built from this meaning is:

"to jockey for position"

This phrase is used so often that it has become almost its own idiom. It means to compete with others — using clever, careful moves — to place yourself in the most advantageous spot. That "spot" can be literal (a physical position) or figurative (a job, a rank, influence, attention, etc.).

3. To manipulate or trick someone into something (less common, but important)

In a darker shade of meaning, "jockey" can also mean to cleverly — and somewhat deceptively — steer a person into doing what you want. Here, the "skill" involved is more like cunning or manipulation.

Examples:

  • He jockeyed her into accepting a lower salary by making her feel lucky to have the job at all.
  • They jockeyed the client into signing before he could consult a lawyer.

Notice that in this sense, the person being jockeyed is often unaware that they are being maneuvered. The word implies subtle, behind-the-scenes steering rather than open, direct pressure.
The Unifying Thread Across All Three Meanings

Whether you are squeezing furniture through a door, competing with colleagues for a promotion, or cunningly steering someone's decisions, the word "jockey" always contains these same three elements:

  • Deliberate effort — it never happens by accident
  • Skill or cleverness — brute force is not the method; smart adjustment is
  • A goal or advantage in mind — there is always something to be gained or achieved
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Jockey" sits in a mildly negative to neutral zone. When someone says people are "jockeying," it often carries a slightly critical or cynical flavour — suggesting that the competition is a little unseemly, self-interested, or even underhanded. It implies people are looking out for themselves and using slick moves to do so. However, it is not a strongly negative word. Describing runners "jockeying for position" in a race, for example, is entirely neutral — it simply describes the competitive maneuvering.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Maneuver — broader and more neutral; "jockey" specifically implies competition or tight constraints
  • Compete — general; "jockey" implies subtler, cleverer, more strategic moves rather than open head-to-head competition
  • Manipulate — darker and more intentional in its deception; "jockey" can be used in that way but doesn't always carry that weight
  • Jostle — this is about physically pushing against others in a crowd; "jockey" is about strategy, not physical pushing
